rows.title: Why the name Taft-Hartley got airplay during the dockworkers' brief strike
rows.standfirst: The U.S. economy is breathing a little easier after the International Longshoremen's Association reached a tentative agreement last week with the United States Maritime Alliance. The short-lived dockworkers strike reignited a debate over whether the president ought to intervene, invoking an old law on the books called the Taft-Hartley Act. On today's show, we explain what the Taft-Hartley Act is, why it was created and why it's still scorned by unions.

rows.title: One possible housing crisis solution? A new kind of public housing for all income levels
rows.standfirst: Maryland's Montgomery County is building mixed-income apartments in which people who can afford to pay market rate allow other renters to pay less. Cities and states nationwide are taking up the idea.

rows.title: 'I’m so grateful to these people.' Latino workers in storm-hit Tennessee feel isolated but hopeful
rows.standfirst: There are barriers preventing many Latino farm workers in northeastern Tennessee from trying to get help, but the extended Latino community is bringing the help to them.

rows.title: A coal power plant demolition serves as a poignant historical moment for the Navajo
rows.standfirst: For six decades, coal has provided for — and polluted — the Navajo Nation. Demolition of a power plant brings mixed emotions.

rows.title: A victim of a crypto ‘pig butchering’ scam just got his $140,000 back
rows.standfirst: NPR investigated a crypto scam company known as SpireBit, which stole hundreds of thousands of dollars from Russian-speaking seniors. Now, some of the victims are getting their money back after a lawsuit by Massachusetts authorities.

rows.title: Does unemployment whiplash mean recession?
rows.standfirst: It's Jobs Friday! It's that time of the month where we check in on the American worker.

rows.title: What's up with all the ads for law firms?
rows.standfirst: The lawyer commercial is almost an art form unto itself. Learned practitioners of the law doing whatever it takes to get your attention, from impressive dirt bike stunts to running around half naked. All so when you land in trouble, you don't have to think hard to remember their name. Odds are you can name one or two right now.

rows.title: The U.S. saw stunningly strong growth in jobs last month. Here's what to know
rows.standfirst: U.S. employers added more than a quarter million jobs in September, while the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. Here's what to know about the data.

rows.title: Dockworkers suspend strike. And, Tyre Nichols' family applauds trial verdict
rows.standfirst: Dockworkers suspended their strike yesterday, avoiding an "economic crisis," but a sticking point remains in negotiations. And, Tyre Nichols trial verdict brings hope for police brutality cases.

rows.title: Port strikes end with deal on wages, averting economic disaster
rows.standfirst: The two sides have agreed to a 62% wage increase over 6 years in a deal between the International Longshoremen's Association and the U.S. Maritime Alliance. The union had been seeking a 77% increase.

rows.title: Champagne. Neapolitan pizza. Now döner kebabs?
rows.standfirst: In Germany, döner kebabs are more than just an affordable, satisfying street food. They're a symbol of Turkey's culinary influence in the country. Today on the show, how an effort to give döner kebabs a protected status under a little-known EU regulation could dish out some real economic consequences, in Germany and beyond.

rows.title: Tensions are rising in the Middle East, but the rise in oil prices is muted – so far
rows.standfirst: Crude oil prices have risen as Iran and Israel trade attacks, but not as much as you might expect. One reason? OPEC+ could pump a lot more oil if it wanted to.

rows.title: 23andMe is on the brink. What happens to all its DNA data?
rows.standfirst: The once-hot Silicon Valley startup has seen its stock’s value decline 99% and is struggling to survive. That has put the spotlight on the genetic data it has on 15 million people.

rows.title: Why bananas may become one of the first casualties of the dockworkers strike
rows.standfirst: One of the first places shoppers may feel the effects of the dockworkers' strike is in the produce aisle. Hundreds of tons of bananas are stuck in transit — and they won't keep for long.

rows.title: How Venezuela imploded (update)
rows.standfirst: (Note: A version of this episode originally ran in 2016.)

rows.title: Lilly Ledbetter, the activist who inspired Fair Pay Act, dies at 86
rows.standfirst: Lilly Ledbetter, a supervisor at a Goodyear tire plant in Alabama, discovered she was receiving less pay than men who worked the same position. Her case led to a monumental law on pay equity.

rows.title: Nobel Prize goes to 3 economists who study the wealth and poverty of nations
rows.standfirst: The award is shared by Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson of MIT and James Robinson of the University of Chicago for their research on the institutional roots of national wealth and poverty. They will split the prize money of 11 million Swedish krona or about $1.058 million.

rows.title: Inside the TikTok documents: Stripping teens and boosting 'attractive' people
rows.standfirst: A trove of secret documents show teens’ increasing reliance on TikTok and how executives were acutely aware of the potential harm the app can cause young people, but appeared unconcerned.

rows.title: 7-Eleven to close over 400 stores in North America
rows.standfirst: The ubiquitous convenience store owed its recent revenue drops to inflation, declining cigarette sales and a shift in palates toward fresh food and specialty drinks.

rows.title: Senators call on TikTok to produce documents in response to NPR report
rows.standfirst: Two senators, who have pushed online child safety legislation in Congress, demanded that TikTok executives share all materials the company has about the dangers kids may encounter on the wildly popular service.

rows.title: Boeing will lay off 10% of employees as a strike shuts down airplane production
rows.standfirst: Boeing has been losing money for over five years and is now dealing with a strike that has shut down factories in the Seattle area. The staff cuts will include executives and managers, the CEO said.

rows.title: So imPORTant: Bananas, frogs, and... Bob's??
rows.standfirst: Even in our modern world with planes and jets and drones, the vast majority of goods are moved around the planet in cargo ships. Which means our ports are the backbone of our global economy. The longshoremans' strike closed the eastern ports for only three days, but those three days raised a lot of questions.

rows.title: The cost of living, lead pipe removal, and a more expensive Mega Millions
rows.standfirst: It's ... Indicators of the Week! It's that time of week when we look at the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: Stellantis, maker of Jeep and Ram, lays off more than 1,000 Detroit workers
rows.standfirst: The international company that owns the American brands is struggling with a glut of unsold cars and smaller profits. The layoffs could have ripple effects through its U.S. workforce of 52,000.

rows.title: Where manufacturing jobs have shrunk, a library is giving a leg up to entrepreneurs
rows.standfirst: The public library in Toledo, Ohio, is one of a number across the U.S. that have become entrepreneurial hubs. Business-specialist librarians are helping aspiring small-business owners and nonprofits for free.

rows.title: Award-winning Ukrainian journalist dies in Russian captivity, Kyiv says
rows.standfirst: Ukrainian officials on Thursday confirmed the death of freelance journalist Victoria Roshchyna, though the circumstances surrounding her death were unclear.

rows.title: TikTok executives know about app’s effect on teens, lawsuit documents allege
rows.standfirst: In communications newly revealed, TikTok executives discuss being aware of the harms caused by their app. TikTok officials were warned of the app’s dangers to minors.

rows.title: SpaceX wants to go to Mars. To get there, environmentalists say it’s trashing Texas
rows.standfirst: With each launch, SpaceX has been discharging tens of thousands of gallons of industrial wastewater into sensitive wetlands. Environmentalists say an increase in launches will only make things worse.

rows.title: TD Bank to pay $3 billion in money-laundering settlement with the Justice Department
rows.standfirst: Canada-based TD Bank pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering, the largest bank in U.S. history to do so, Attorney General Merrick Garland said.

rows.title: Infant swings recalled after deaths
rows.standfirst: The deaths of five infants ages 1-3 months old occurred from 2012 to 2022. It's not the first time the New York-based company has had to remove products from the market following infant fatalities.

rows.title: 6 Indian airline flights declare emergencies amid spate of fake bomb threats
rows.standfirst: Six flights from India declared emergencies within 30 minutes of each other. It comes as fake bomb threats are causing disruptions, diversions and delays for scores of flights on Indian airlines.

rows.title: It's Love Week! How the TV holiday rom-com got so successful
rows.standfirst: Welcome to Love Week on the Indicator, our weeklong series exploring the business and economic side of romance. On today's show, we fire up the gas logs and pour a mug of cocoa to discuss the made-for-TV rom-com machine, and how television executives learned to mass produce seasonal romance.

rows.title: Boeing union is set to vote on a new contract deal, possibly ending strike
rows.standfirst: The latest proposal includes a 35% general wage increase over four years — bringing it closer to the union's original ask for 40%. Boeing previously offered a 25% raise over the life of the contract.

rows.title: Frozen waffles sold at Walmart, Target and supermarkets are recalled over listeria risk
rows.standfirst: The recall includes various certain frozen waffles sold in Walmart, Target, Publix and other stores. Some waffles for brands like Kodiak Cakes, Simple Truth and Food Hold have also been recalled.

rows.title: U.S. to probe Tesla's 'Full Self-Driving' system after pedestrian killed
rows.standfirst: The U.S. government's road safety agency is investigating Tesla's “Full Self-Driving” system after getting reports of crashes in low-visibility conditions, including one that killed a pedestrian.

rows.title: The Subscription Trap
rows.standfirst: Over the past two decades, there's been a sort of tectonic economic shift happening under our feet. More and more companies have switched from selling goods one by one to selling services, available as a subscription. These days everything from razor blades to meal kits to car washes have become subscriptions. But all that convenience has also come with a dark side – some companies have designed their offerings to be as easy as possible to sign up for and also as difficult as possible to cancel. Many consumers are now paying for way more subscriptions than they even know about.

rows.title: Reversing shrinkflation (via potato chips) and other indicators
rows.standfirst: It's ... Indicators of the Week! It's that time of week where we look at the most intriguing indicators from this last week of economic and business news.

rows.title: CVS Health CEO Lynch steps down as the drugstore chain struggles to right its path
rows.standfirst: CVS Health CEO Karen Lynch has stepped down, with company shares sinking 19% this year. CVS Health also warned of disappointing third-quarter earnings.

rows.title: Mortgage rates were supposed to come down. Instead, they're rising. Here's why
rows.standfirst: Mortgage rates are ticking up, even after the Federal Reserve has started cutting interest rates. Here's why, and where rates — and home sales — could go from here.

rows.title: Rebranding 'the world's most dangerous private army'
rows.standfirst: When the leader of the Wagner group, Yevgeny Prigozhin died in an exploding plane widely attributed to Russian President Vladimir Putin, it wasn't clear what would happen. Today, why the Wagner Group has been called the world's most dangerous private army, its relationship with Russia and how its business model creates a blueprint for others to follow.

rows.title: New records show Texas judge on X case didn't sell his Tesla shares after taking the suit
rows.standfirst: The judge, Reed O’Connor, in Fort Worth, Texas, has rejected calls for him to step down from the high-profile case Musk filed against Media Matters, a watchdog group.

rows.title: Former county official gets at least 28 years in prison for killing Las Vegas reporter
rows.standfirst: Robert Telles, a former Las Vegas-area official, was sentenced for killing Jeff German, who wrote articles critical of his conduct in office and exposed an intimate relationship with a coworker.

rows.title: Can the yield curve still predict recessions?
rows.standfirst: Two years ago, the yield curve inverted. That means short-term interest rates on Treasury bonds were unusually higher than long-term interest rates. When that's happened in the past, a recession has come. In fact, the inverted yield curve has predicted every recession since 1969 ... until now. Today, are we saying goodbye to the inverted yield curve's flawless record?

rows.title: Canceling subscriptions has to be as easy as signing up, the FTC says in a new rule
rows.standfirst: The "click-to-cancel" rule, now finalized by the Federal Trade Commission, aims to make it easier to cancel subscriptions and memberships. Companies argue that the agency overstepped its authority.

rows.title: Millions of pounds of meat are being recalled. Here's what to look for in your fridge
rows.standfirst: Over 11 million pounds of ready-to-eat meat and poultry were recalled over listeria concerns, affecting salads, wraps, frozen meals and more from popular chains like Target, Trader Joe's and Walmart.

rows.title: Housing is expensive. Here's how Harris and Trump promise to bring costs down
rows.standfirst: Housing costs are a top issue for many voters. Former President Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris have proposed different ideas for addressing the country's housing woes.

rows.title: The U.S. once banned Chinese immigrants — and it paid an economic price
rows.standfirst: In 1880, the Chinese were the biggest group of immigrants in the western U.S. But Sinophobic sentiments crystallized into racist policies and eventually the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. The rationale was that banning Chinese laborers would boost job opportunities for U.S.-born workers. Today, an economist explains how the Chinese exclusion laws affected the economies of western states and what it says about our current debate over immigration and jobs.

rows.title: Why abortion referendums are also about the economy
rows.standfirst: Abortion is on the ballot in 10 states. The vote results will have consequences beyond women's reproductive rights.

rows.title: So your data was stolen in a data breach
rows.standfirst: If you... exist in the world, it's likely that you have gotten a letter or email at some point informing you that your data was stolen. This happened recently to potentially hundreds of millions of people in a hack that targeted companies like Ticketmaster, AT&T, Advance Auto Parts and others that use the data cloud company Snowflake.

rows.title: An Elon Musk-backed political group is posting fake Kamala Harris ads on Facebook
rows.standfirst: Ads seemingly advocating for Vice President Harris on Facebook are really part of an effort by a dark money group to mislead voters. The messages have been viewed millions of times.

rows.title: What's missing in the immigration debate
rows.standfirst: Immigration is a top concern among U.S. voters this election cycle. But Zeke Hernandez, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania who studies immigration,thinks politicians and the media aren't giving the public the full story. Too often, he argues, they paint immigrants as objects of pity or fear, when the reality is much more complex — and positive. Today on the show, we look beyond the binary and explore the less talked about ways documented and undocumented immigrants shape the U.S. economy.

rows.title: The U.S. economy is growing solidly. Here's what's working — and what's not
rows.standfirst: The U.S. economy grew at an annual rate of 2.8% in the third quarter, led by strong consumer spending. The news comes days before a presidential election in which the economy has been top of mind for many voters.

rows.title: Union workers could decide this election — and their unions know it
rows.standfirst: With much at stake on Election Day, labor unions have deployed canvassers to knock on doors in swing states. With polling tight, the focus is on turning out the vote.

rows.title: Starbucks hopes faster drinks, fewer upcharges and nicer mugs bring people back
rows.standfirst: Shoppers complain that Starbucks isn't fancy enough — but they also say it's too expensive. The new CEO, Brian Niccol, is ordering up big changes.

rows.title: What happens when Social Security runs out of money?
rows.standfirst: Social Security has thus far been self-sustaining—payroll taxes go into this big fund, which then pays out monthly checks. But the problem we have now is the money coming into that fund is not keeping up with the money going out.

rows.title: JPMorgan Chase is suing customers over 'infinite money glitch' ATM scam
rows.standfirst: JPMorgan Chase is filing lawsuits against customers who exploited a viral technical glitch this summer that allowed people to pull huge amounts from Chase ATMs.

rows.title: Many sports fans really miss paper tickets. Now, teams are tapping into that demand
rows.standfirst: There's one thing that many sports and music fans miss in this digital age: the physical, paper tickets of the recent past. And now, they are making a bit of a comeback.

rows.title: Why you’re seeing scary-high chocolate candy prices this Halloween
rows.standfirst: Don't be surprised if you see fewer chocolate treats in your trick-or-treating loot. Customers are souring on costly chocolate, resulting from a few disappointing cocoa crop years.

rows.title: Over 200,000 subscribers flee 'Washington Post' after Bezos blocks Harris endorsement
rows.standfirst: Over 200,000 people canceled their subscriptions in the first few days following news that The Washington Post would not endorse any presidential candidate.

rows.title: What looks like a bond and acts like a bond but isn't a bond?
rows.standfirst: The Maldives is a small island nation struggling with a heavy debt load. Its borrowing includes $500 million worth of something called sukuk. These are bond-like investments that don't pay interest, to be in line with Islamic law. Today on the show, we explain how sukuk works, how it fits into the larger world of Islamic finance and what might happen if the Maldives can't pay back its debt.

frame: Up to15 visible Business-archive cards at four fixed weekly endpoints, restricted to each block; not a full-publication census
